title: Cells as Systems
subject: Science
developmentNotes: High-school biology should move beyond organelle memorization into system interactions, structure/function, inputs/outputs, and evidence from models.
learningObjective: Students will model a cell as a system, explain how organelles interact, and use structure-function reasoning to support claims.
essentialQuestion: How do cell parts work together to keep the cell alive?

vocabularyTerms.definition: a specialized structure inside a cell
organelle that stores DNA and helps control cell activities
organelles that release usable energy from food molecules
boundary that controls what enters and leaves
a set of interacting parts that form a whole

prerequisites: Know living things are made of cells

hook.content: Students compare a cell to a city or factory model, then critique where the analogy works and where it breaks down.
hook.studentAction: Predict, notice, or explain initial thinking before direct instruction.
hook.teacherOrAppAction: Capture initial response as non-graded diagnostic evidence.

learningGoal.content: I can students will model a cell as a system, explain how organelles interact, and use structure-function reasoning to support claims.
successCriteria: I can explain the core concept in my own words.
I can show evidence or reasoning, not only an answer.

miniTeach.content: A cell is a system because it has interacting parts. The membrane controls exchange, DNA provides instructions, ribosomes build proteins, mitochondria release usable energy, and other structures support transport and storage. If one part fails, the whole system can be affected.
miniTeach.cognitiveLoadNotes: Use short chunks, one example at a time, and reveal labels only after students observe the model.

firstPrinciplesBreakdown.coreConcept: A cell survives through coordinated interactions among specialized parts.
known: Cells exchange materials with the environment.
unknown: How failure of one organelle affects the system.
rules: Systems depend on interactions, not isolated parts.
Inputs and outputs must be regulated.
avoid: Do not memorize organelles as disconnected facts.
Do not treat the cell as a machine with no chemical processes.
steps: Name the organelle or structure involved.
Connect it to another cell part.
Predict system effects if it fails.
firstPrinciplesBreakdown.check: A strong explanation uses both structure/function and interaction with other parts.

workedExample.content: Claim: The cell membrane helps maintain cell stability. Evidence: It forms a boundary and controls what enters and leaves. Reasoning: By regulating materials, the membrane helps the cell get needed substances and remove waste without losing internal balance.
workedExample.teacherOrAppAction: Highlight each reasoning step and connect it to the first-principles breakdown.

items: Label a cell diagram by function rather than name only.
Match organelle failures to likely system effects.
Explain how nucleus, ribosomes, and proteins connect.
guidedPractice.scaffolding: Start with high support, then remove hints. Require explanation on the final item.

evidenceBasedReasoningTask.prompt: Claim: Cells are systems. Use two organelle interactions as evidence.

activePractice.content: Students build a systems map linking organelles, inputs, outputs, and consequences of failure.

reteachPath.misconception: Student memorizes organelle names without understanding interactions.
reteachPath.simpleExplanation: A cell is not just a list of parts; it is a system where each part affects other parts.
steps: Identify which part helps meet it.
Connect it to another organelle or process.
Predict what happens if it fails.

practice.answer: Cells are systems of interacting parts.

reteachPath.exitCriteria: Student completes at least 4 of 5 reteach items and explains the corrected misconception.

tasks: Compare a plant cell and animal cell as systems.
Critique a city analogy for a cell and identify two limitations.
Predict effects of a membrane transport problem on cell stability.
challengePath.extensionRule: Unlock at 90+ mastery or teacher/parent assignment; still schedule Memory Vault review.

successCriteria: I can identify cell structures and functions.
I can explain how parts work together as a system.
I can use evidence from a model or image.
I can predict how a changed part affects the system.

knowledge: Cells contain interacting structures that support life functions.
capability: Build and interpret a labeled cell-system model.
reasoning: Connect structure, function, and system effects.
retention: Recall cell structures and functions after a delay.
transfer: Apply systems reasoning to a new cell, tissue, or biological process.

phaseModules.title: Enter the cell lab
phaseModules.studentAction: Observe a cell image and predict what parts must do to keep the cell functioning.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can state a structure-function question.

phaseModules.title: See the cell as a system
phaseModules.studentAction: Follow a labeled model connecting membrane, nucleus, organelles, inputs, and outputs.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can connect a part to a job.

phaseModules.title: Sort structure and function
phaseModules.studentAction: Match cell parts to functions and identify evidence for each match.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can explain why a match fits.

phaseModules.title: Build the system model
phaseModules.studentAction: Assemble a labeled cell model and trace one material or signal through it.
phaseModules.successCheck: The model shows interactions, not a parts list only.

phaseModules.title: Test a changed part
phaseModules.studentAction: Predict how a damaged or missing structure could affect the cell and defend the prediction.
phaseModules.successCheck: I connect change, function, and system effect.

phaseModules.title: Explain a new cell model
phaseModules.studentAction: Answer questions and explain structure-function evidence independently.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve the system map
phaseModules.studentAction: Reconstruct key structures and functions after a delay.

phaseModules.title: Scale the system idea
phaseModules.studentAction: Apply structure-function reasoning to tissues, organs, or a new cell type.

phaseModules.title: Repair or extend
phaseModules.studentAction: Fix a missing interaction or extend the model with a new input or output.
phaseModules.successCheck: My next move addresses the system evidence.

proofTasks.prompt: Name key cell structures and functions.
Explain how one cell part supports a system function.
Build and explain a new cell-system model.
Retrieve structure-function relationships after a delay.
Apply systems reasoning to a new biological level.

feedbackRules.result: The learner names structures without functions or interactions.
feedbackRules.hint: Ask what the part does and what would change without it.

feedbackRules.result: The learner assigns a function without model evidence.
feedbackRules.hint: Point to the structure or flow that supports the claim.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner cannot connect a structure to a function.
reteachPaths.action: Use three labeled structure-function cards and trace one interaction.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot distinguish cell, tissue, and organ levels.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Sort biological organization cards before returning to the cell system.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner explains a cell model independently.
challengePaths.action: Model how a changed input affects two connected structures and the system output.

parentTeacherNotes: Ask the student to explain a cell part using “Its job is ___, and it affects the cell by ___.”
accessibilityNotes: Use plain, grade-appropriate language and define academic vocabulary before using it in prompts.
Provide alt text or text-equivalent descriptions for every image, diagram, array, chart, map, or model.
Make all interactive elements keyboard accessible with visible focus states and screen-reader labels.
Never rely only on color to communicate correct/incorrect, categories, or importance.
Provide read-aloud support for Foundation Academy and optional read-aloud for all grade bands.
Chunk instructions into short steps and provide examples before independent work.
safetyNotes: No public student posting, random direct messages, or unrestricted discussion.
Discussion prompts must use sentence frames and moderation/teacher controls when implemented.
Student-generated work should be visible only to the student and authorized parent/teacher roles unless explicitly assigned in a safe classroom workflow.
Do not collect unnecessary personal information in lesson responses.
implementationNotes: Render lessonFlow sections in order with progress state.
Persist quiz attempts and item-level skill tags.
Generate Memory Vault records after lesson completion.
Use mastery bands to branch to reteach, guided practice, review, or challenge.
Store open responses privately with role-based access.
Use answer keys and rubrics for review; do not expose hidden answer keys in student mode.
